turns.prompt_text: I am looking for different terminals to use on mac, I've seen warp, it looks promising, should I give it a try?
turns.response_html:
Warp is indeed "promising," but it is also one of the most polarizing tools in the developer community right now.

To give you a well-rounded answer, I have gathered perspectives from different corners of the tech world—ranging from privacy advocates and "old school" sysadmins to modern product-focused developers—so you can decide where you fit in.

The Short Answer

Yes, give it a try if you want a "modern" experience that feels more like a code editor (VS Code) than a traditional terminal, and you value out-of-the-box AI features over total privacy or configurability.

No, skip it if you rely heavily on tmux, hate forced logins, or prefer open-source software that you can audit yourself.

Perspective 1: The "Modern Workflow" Developer

  • The Vibe: "I want my tools to be smart and help me write commands faster."
  • Why they love Warp:
    • The Input Area: Unlike a standard terminal where you type at the very bottom, Warp uses a fixed text-editor-like input box. You can use mouse clicks to move the cursor, select text, and use standard shortcuts (Cmd+C/V) easily.
    • AI Integration: It has built-in AI (Warp AI) that can explain error messages or write commands for you (e.g., "how do I undo the last git commit?").
    • Blocks: Output is grouped into "blocks." You can copy just the output of one command without accidentally selecting the prompt or the next command.
    • Team Features: You can share a "block" of code/output with a colleague via a web link.

Perspective 2: The "Privacy & Open Source" Purist

  • The Vibe: "I don't want my terminal sending data to the cloud, and I want to own my tools."
  • Why they dislike Warp:
    • Forced Login: This is the #1 complaint in communities like Hacker News and Reddit. You must log in to use Warp, even for local shell work. Many developers feel a terminal should be a local-only utility.
    • Telemetry: It collects data. While Warp says this is for product improvement and can be toggled, the closed-source nature makes it harder for the community to verify exactly what is being sent.
    • Closed Source: Unlike almost every other terminal emulator, Warp is proprietary.

Perspective 3: The "Performance & Customization" Tinkerer

  • The Vibe: "I want my terminal to run at 144Hz, use zero RAM, and be configured via a config file."
  • The Friction with Warp:
    • Resource Usage: Because it tries to do so much (AI, graphical blocks), it can be heavier on system resources than minimal emulators.
    • Non-Standard: It breaks some traditional shell assumptions. If you use tools like tmux (terminal multiplexer) or highly customized Zsh plugins, Warp often conflicts with them or renders them useless because it "takes over" the shell experience.

The Alternatives (What others are using)

If Warp's "forced login" or "non-standard" nature turns you off, here is what the other camps are using on Mac:

TerminalBest For...The Consensus
iTerm2The StandardThe reliable workhorse. It has 90% of the features you'll ever need, is open-source, and extremely stable. It's the "safe" choice for professionals.
GhosttyThe New ContenderCurrently gaining massive hype. It combines the speed of Alacritty with the native Mac feel of iTerm. It is fast, uses native UI, and is built by Mitchell Hashimoto (creator of Terraform/Vagrant).
Alacritty / KittyThe Speed FreaksGPU-accelerated and hyper-minimal. You configure them via text files (YAML/Lua). They are blazing fast but offer zero hand-holding.
WaveThe Open AlternativeIf you like Warp's "editor" feel and blocks but want something open-source, Wave is a newer project attempting to do similar things without the proprietary lock-in.

Recommendation

Since you are curious, download Warp and use it for a week, but keep your current terminal installed.

Look for this specific friction: Does the "Input Box" feel helpful, or does it feel like it's fighting your muscle memory? If you find yourself fighting it, switch to Ghostty or stick with iTerm2.

turns.prompt_text: I have warp installed, however I am having trouble, the initialization is not ocurring
turns.response_html:
When Warp hangs on initialization (often stuck on "Starting shell..." or just a blank screen), it is almost always due to a conflict with your existing shell configuration (.zshrc or .bashrc) or a network/login handshake failure.

Here is a troubleshooting guide broken down by the most likely culprits.

1. The "Shell Configuration" Angle (Most Likely)

Since you are a developer with an existing setup, your .zshrc or .bashrc likely contains plugins, custom prompts (like Powerlevel10k), or eval statements that are conflicting with Warp's wrapper.

The Test: Launch a standard terminal (Terminal.app or iTerm2) and temporarily rename your configuration file to see if Warp starts with a "clean" shell.

mv ~/.zshrc ~/.zshrc_backup
# OR if you use bash
mv ~/.bashrc ~/.bashrc_backup
  • If Warp starts successfully: You know the issue is inside your config file.
  • The Fix: You don't have to delete your config. You can tell your shell to skip certain plugins when running inside Warp by wrapping them in this conditional:
if [[ $TERM_PROGRAM != "WarpTerminal" ]]; then
    # Put conflicting plugins/prompts here
    # e.g., source ~/powerlevel10k/powerlevel10k.zsh-theme
fi

(After testing, remember to restore your file: mv ~/.zshrc_backup ~/.zshrc)

2. The "Network & Auth" Angle

Warp is unique because it requires an initial handshake with its servers to log you in. If this hangs, the terminal never initializes.

  • Firewall/VPN: If you are on a strict corporate VPN (like at a large enterprise) or use software like Little Snitch, ensure Warp is allowed to contact api.warp.dev.
  • Stale Login Token: Sometimes the local authentication token gets corrupted.
    • Fix: Open Spotlight (Cmd + Space), type "Keychain Access," and open it. Search for warp and delete any entries like dev.warp.Warp-Stable. Restart Warp to force a fresh login.

3. The "SSH Wrapper" Angle

If you are trying to SSH into a server immediately or have SSH configs that auto-connect: Warp tries to "wrap" SSH sessions to enable its features (blocks, AI) on the remote server. This wrapper often fails on non-standard remote shells.

  • Fix: Go to Settings > Features and disable Warp SSH Wrapper.

4. The "Ghost in the Machine" (Zsh Startup Files)

Sometimes the issue isn't your main config, but the system-wide startup files. Warp injects a bootstrap script here.

  • Check your .zprofile or .zlogin files. If they have interactive commands (commands that wait for user input, like a password prompt or read command), Warp will hang indefinitely waiting for input that you can't see.

Summary Checklist to Unstick It

  1. [ ] Force Quit Warp completely (Cmd+Q).
  2. [ ] Rename ~/.zshrc temporarily to ~/.zshrc_backup.
  3. [ ] Open Warp.
    • If it works: The issue is a plugin in your rc file. Restore the file and comment out plugins one by one (start with heavy prompt themes).
    • If it still fails: It is likely a network/auth issue. Delete the keychain entry or check your VPN.

Next Step: Would you like me to help you identify which specific plugin in your .zshrc might be causing the conflict?

turns.prompt_text: warp does not like tmux does it?
turns.response_html:
You are spot on. Warp and tmux are effectively enemies.

They technically "run" together, but they fight over the same territory. If you are a heavy tmux user, Warp will likely feel like a downgrade.

The Core Conflict

Warp isn't just a window that displays text; it fundamentally changes how the shell works by intercepting your keystrokes to provide its "Input Editor" and "Blocks."

Tmux does the exact same thing. It intercepts input to manage panes and windows. When you run tmux inside Warp, you create a "tug-of-war":

  • Warp loses its brain: Inside a tmux session, Warp cannot distinguish where a command starts or ends. It turns into a "dumb" terminal—you lose the AI, the mouse support, the copy/paste blocks, and the text editor input.
  • Tmux loses its keys: Warp’s native shortcuts (like Cmd+D to split panes) often conflict with tmux bindings, or Warp swallows the key presses before tmux sees them.

The "Warp Way" vs. The "Tmux Way"

FeatureThe Warp WayThe Tmux WayThe Friction
Window ManagementNative Tabs & Panes (Cmd+D)Virtual Panes (Ctrl+b %)Warp wants you to use its panes. It does not support tmux control mode.
Persistence"Warp Drive" (Cloud history)Detach/Attach SessionsWarp has no "detach" feature. If you close the window, the session dies.
InputIDE-style Text BoxStandard StreamTmux forces Warp to revert to a standard stream, disabling Warp's best feature.

The Verdict

  • If you use tmux for local window management (splitting panes): You should try to drop tmux and use Warp's native splits (Cmd+D and Cmd+Shift+D). They are smoother and mouse-friendly, but you lose the scriptability of tmux.

  • If you use tmux for remote persistence (keeping sessions alive on servers): Warp is the wrong tool. You will have a better experience with Ghostty or WezTerm. These terminals are built to integrate with tmux, not replace it.

Quick check: Do you use tmux mainly to keep remote sessions alive (SSH), or just to organize your screen locally?
